Medina Festival of Tunis

Evening concerts of traditional and tarab music, theatre and workshops in the old town of Tunis during Ramadan; the 42nd edition was in 2026. It follows Ramadan, so it comes about eleven days earlier each year.
Festival of the Saharan Ksour

A spring festival of southern Berber heritage, founded in 1979: folk shows, horsemanship and a crafts fair around the fortified granaries. It has been irregular: it paused after 2022, and a revival was announced for March 2026.
Ghriba pilgrimage

The yearly Jewish pilgrimage to the El Ghriba synagogue on Djerba, around Lag BaOmer, with prayers and processions. Its date follows the Hebrew calendar; it has been smaller since 2023 and is held under tight security.
Falconry Festival of El Haouaria
Three days on Cap Bon where local falconers show and compete with trained sparrowhawks and falcons. Held each June; 2025 was the 56th edition.
Tabarka Jazz Festival
Jazz, world and contemporary music on the north coast since 1973, with free street jazz in the evenings. It came back in July 2026 after a six-year break, so it is not held every year.
Dougga Festival
Summer concerts in the Roman theatre of Dougga, mostly Tunisian artists. Held most summers; the 50th edition ran over ten evenings in July 2026.
Malouf Festival of Testour
A week of malouf, the Arab-Andalusian music of Tunisia, in the Andalusian town of Testour, since 1967. Usually in July, but the 2026 edition was cancelled.
Aoussou Carnival
Sousse’s summer carnival: floats, brass bands and folk troupes from Tunisia and abroad, traditionally on 24 July near Boujaafar beach.
International Festival of Carthage
Tunisia’s best-known summer festival, every July and August since 1964 in the Roman theatre of Carthage: concerts by Arab and international artists, some theatre and dance.
Hammamet International Festival
Music and stage shows since 1964 in an open-air amphitheatre of 1,000 seats above the Gulf of Hammamet, through July and August.
El Jem Symphonic Music Festival
Orchestras from Tunisia and abroad play inside the Roman amphitheatre of El Jem, every summer since the mid-1980s.
Sfax International Festival
Concerts, shows and films in the open-air theatre of Sfax, from late July to mid-August; 2026 was the 46th edition.
Kerkennah Festival
A popular summer festival on the Kerkennah islands: music, comedy, rap and shows for children. The 30th edition was in summer 2025.
Mouled in Kairouan
Hundreds of thousands come to Kairouan for the Prophet’s birthday, with free shows and light displays over about a week. It follows the Islamic calendar: late August in 2026, then earlier each year.
Carthage Theatre Days
A theatre festival since 1983, with more than 80 shows from Tunisia, the Arab world and Africa, mostly at the City of Culture in Tunis. Recent editions were in late November.
Carthage Film Festival
African and Arab cinema in Tunis since 1966, with the Tanit d’or award. Traditionally October–November; recent editions were in December.
International Festival of the Sahara
Four days of desert life at the end of December in Douz: camel races, horsemanship, a Bedouin wedding, poetry and music, at the edge of the dunes.
Festival of the Oases
Late December in Tozeur, first held in 1938: the oases and the date harvest, with concerts, horsemanship, street arts and date markets.

Called kosksi at home: semolina steamed over a stew, served with vegetables and meat or fish that change with the region and the season. Its know-how is on the UNESCO list of intangible heritage since 2020, shared with Algeria, Mauritania and Morocco.
A paper-thin sheet of malsouka pastry folded around a filling and fried until crisp. The classic hides a whole egg with tuna, onion, parsley and harissa.
Chickpeas in a garlic and cumin broth over pieces of bread, topped with harissa, olive oil, egg, capers or tuna. Once a winter breakfast, now eaten at any hour.
Eggs cooked in a spicy sauce of tomatoes, green chillies and harissa, often with merguez sausage. Mop it up with bread.
Kairouan and Tunis, each with its own recipe
Fried peppers and tomatoes chopped together with eggs, eaten by dipping bread. Kairouan’s is very spicy; the Tunis one adds pumpkin.
Cap Bon, above all Nabeul
Tunisia’s chilli paste: sun-dried peppers ground with salt, garlic and coriander. It seasons everyday food and is on the UNESCO list of intangible heritage since 2022.
A dark green sauce of powdered mulukhiyah leaves slowly cooked in olive oil with beef or lamb, eaten with bread.
Kairouan
Small diamonds of semolina filled with dates. They come from Kairouan, which held the first national makroudh festival in 2008.
Sidi Bou Said
A fried doughnut dusted with sugar or soaked in honey. Sidi Bou Said is famous for it.
Sweet mint tea poured over pine nuts in the glass; almonds or peanuts sometimes take their place.
A small fried roll filled with tuna, egg, potato, olives, capers, preserved lemon and harissa: the classic street snack.
Its name means “mixed”: a stew of tomatoes, peppers, onions and garlic, often with eggs.
The oases of the Djerid and Nefzaoua
Soft, honey-sweet dates, the “dates of light”, grown in the desert oases. They also fill the makroudh.
Sfax
Olive oil is central to life around Sfax, which makes about 40% of Tunisia’s. The geographer al-Idrisi praised its olives in the 12th century.

Visas and passports
No visa for up to 90 days for most of the EU, the UK, the US, Canada, Switzerland, Norway, Russia, China, the Gulf states, Algeria, Libya and Morocco.
Ukrainians normally need a visa, except on an organised tour with a hotel voucher.
Bring your passport: identity cards are not accepted. The UK asks for a passport valid for the whole stay; Canada advises six months beyond departure.
Officers may ask for a return ticket and where you are staying. There is no e-visa: a visa, when needed, comes from a Tunisian embassy.
Rules change and depend on your nationality: check with the Tunisian embassy before booking.
Money
The dinar (TND) is a closed currency: you cannot bring dinars in or take them out. Change money after you land.
Change at banks, licensed exchange offices, hotels or post offices, with your passport. Keep the receipts: you need them to change dinars back before you leave.
Cash machines are common in towns and take Visa and Mastercard. Many hotels and restaurants take cards; taxis, louages, markets and small places want cash.
Hotels charge a small tourist tax per person and night, for up to ten nights.
Safety
Most visits are trouble-free, but the UK, US and Canadian governments ask travellers to stay alert to the risk of terrorism, at tourist and religious sites and in crowds.
Theft is the most common crime: keep valuables out of sight. Avoid demonstrations, and carry a copy of your passport.
Drones need a permit. Follow the flags on the beach.
Health
Tap water is treated in the cities and on the coast; bottled water is cheap and wiser in the countryside and the south.
Ask a travel clinic about hepatitis A and typhoid. Take insurance that covers treatment and repatriation: clinics expect payment on the spot.
Pharmacies are common in towns. Bring your medicines in their boxes with a doctor’s note.
Inland summers are very hot: drink often, cover up and rest at midday. Do not touch stray dogs; get care at once after a bite.
Emergency numbers
Police: 197. National Guard (countryside): 193.
Ambulance: 190. Fire and road accidents: 198.
For a lost passport, call your embassy in Tunis.
Phone and internet
Three networks: Ooredoo, Orange and Tunisie Telecom, with counters in the arrivals hall of Tunis–Carthage. A SIM needs your passport itself, not a copy.
A travel eSIM can be set up before you leave. Hotels and cafés in towns usually have Wi-Fi.
The country code is +216, then eight digits.
Electricity
230 V, 50 Hz, with two round pins (types C and E): a continental European plug fits.
Summer heat can cause short power cuts.
From the airport
Tunis–Carthage: bus 635 to Tunis Marine every 30–40 minutes by day, cash on board; or a yellow taxi with the meter on. Ride apps work too.
Enfidha–Hammamet: no train. Agree the taxi fare before you set off; package holidays usually include the transfer.
Monastir: the Sahel Metro stops 150 m from the terminal, with trains to Monastir, Sousse and Mahdia.
Djerba: taxis to Houmt Souk and the hotels; ask for the meter.
Getting around
Louages are shared minibuses between towns. They leave when full, at fixed fares; a red stripe means long distance.
Trains run from Tunis to Sousse, Monastir and Sfax; allow for delays. In Tunis, the TGM light railway goes to La Goulette, Carthage, Sidi Bou Said and La Marsa.
Driving is on the right. Bring your licence and an international permit, and expect police checkpoints.
Avoid driving at night: poor lighting, animals on the road and unmarked speed bumps.
Customs
Beachwear is fine at the resorts; cover up in towns, at religious sites and in the more conservative south.
Most working mosques are closed to non-Muslims; the courtyards of the Great Mosques of Kairouan, Sousse and Mahdia can be visited. Mind prayer times, above all on Friday at noon.
Do not photograph police, military or government buildings, and ask before photographing people.
Bargaining is normal in the souks; state craft shops have fixed prices, a useful guide. A tip of about 10% is usual in restaurants.
Shops do not sell alcohol on Fridays or during Ramadan; licensed hotels and bars still serve it.
Time, holidays and Ramadan
GMT+1 all year, with no summer time.
Ramadan 2027 is expected from about 8 February to 8 March, depending on the moon. Many restaurants open only at sunset; do not eat, drink or smoke in public by day.
Public holidays: 1 January, 20 March, 9 April, 1 May, 25 July, 13 August, 15 October and 17 December, plus the two Eids, the Islamic New Year and the Prophet’s birthday.
Language
Arabic is the official language; people speak Tunisian Arabic, called Tounsi or Derja.
French is widely spoken and most signs are in Arabic and French. English is common in hotels and tourist places, less elsewhere.
